articles.title: China launches crewed spaceship carrying first Pakistani astronaut to its space station
articles.summary: Beijing/Jiuquan: China on Wednesday launched its Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship carrying three astronauts, including Pakistan 's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national to participate in the country's crewed space programme. The spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, with officials declaring the launch successful minutes later. The crew comprises mission commander and spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and Ali, who will become the first foreign astronaut to visit China's orbiting Tiangong space station. Ali will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft after spending about a week in orbit, while Chinese astronauts typically stay at the station for about six months. The spacecraft is expected to dock with the Tiangong space station in about three hours. India’s Nepal reset faces a China test China built its own space station after it was reportedly excluded from the International Space Station (ISS) over concerns about the involvement of its military, the People's Liberation Army (PLA), in its space programme. China is currently the only country operating its own space station, which became operational in 2022. Tiangong is relatively small compared to the football pitch-sized ISS, where astronauts from several countries have conducted more than 3,000 experiments since its launch in 1998. NASA plans to retire the ISS in early 2031, using a dedicated deorbit vehicle being developed by SpaceX to guide it into a controlled re-entry over the South Pacific, according to reports. The Shenzhou-24 mission's main objectives include completing an in-orbit crew rotation with the Shenzhou-23 crew, maintaining routine station operations, conducting scientific research and carrying out maintenance, public outreach and payload tests, Chinese officials said. More than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests are planned during the mission. These will cover space life sciences, materials science, microgravity fluid physics, combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine and new space technologies, the officials said.

articles.summary: New Delhi: The Samajwadi Party on Tuesday announced its first list of five candidates for the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections even as seat-sharing discussions with the Congress continue. SP's list of five includes Umar Ali Khan from Behat (Saharanpur), Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana (Shamli), Mehboob Ali from Amroha and Jyoti Lodhi from Lalitpur. Earlier on the day, the Akhilesh Yadav-led party offered 26 seats to its I.N.D.I.A ally, an offer that “enraged” the Congress. Nonetheless, both parties displayed a united face after the second round of negotiations on Tuesday. In what is seen as an effort to douse any trouble in the alliance, Akhilesh posted on ‘X’ in the evening, "We have started with 26 winnable seats. Working together wisely, things will move forward." What Azam Khan’s return means for Uttar Pradesh politics The second day of negotiations started soon after SP General Secretary and chief negotiator Ramgopal Yadav told reporters that they had proposed 26 seats to the Congress — two of which it won, four seats where it came second and 20 seats where SP polled 60,000-70,000 votes and the Congress around 2,000 votes. SP’s offer of 26 seats comes at a time when the Congress has been pushing for 131 seats — down from 181 as claimed by Akhilesh. The Congress has now scaled down to 100 seats, sources said. At the meeting, the Congress leaders expressed unhappiness over SP leaders talking publicly about the 26-seat offer, the sources added. After the nearly three-and-half-hour-long meeting, Yadav said the discussions had been positive. "However, 403 seats are a very large number, aren’t they? So, the discussions have not yet been completed,” he added. The Congress’ UP in-charge, Rajendra Pal Gautam, too, said they have a detailed discussion on all seats and that “there were no demands made, as we want to fight unitedly”.

articles.summary: Christchurch: Stumped by the absolute flat track in the opening Test in Wellington, both India and New Zealand will be hoping for a more sporting pitch in the winner-takes-all second and final game, which kicks off at Hagley Oval from Friday. Apart from the triumphant team taking the series spoils 1-0, the second Test has a lot riding on it for both teams, particularly India, who can’t afford any more slip-ups in the World Test Championship (WTC) final race, which is nearing the final bend. India, who have contested two of the three WTC finals and lost both of them, are currently placed fourth in the standings with 50.00 percentage points (PCT), with inaugural champions New Zealand a rung above at 66.67. Holders South Africa are on top at 75.00, while second edition winners Australia are placed below them at 69.23. Given how far India are even behind New Zealand, the top teams after the end of the cycle will contest the final from June 9-13, 2027, at The Oval in London. It is imperative for India to gain maximum points from the second Test. Nothing less than a win could seriously jeopardise their chances of making the final cut. A loss here could be a hammer blow, although they will have one final attempt when they host Australia for five Tests from January. India, whose bowlers sent down 120 overs in the second innings at Basin Reserve following 121 in the first, chose not to train on Wednesday, a day after arriving in Christchurch. Fair enough, because they toiled really hard on an unresponsive pitch, which even New Zealand skipper Tom Latham called "not the traditional Basin Reserve surface". So, what does Hagley Oval look like? The signs are that it will offer assistance to pacers for the opening day or two before settling down into a good batting surface, with runs on offer for those who apply themselves. For the record, the last Test played here saw West Indies pull off a draw by scoring 457/6. Both New Zealand and West Indies didn’t score big in the first innings but made over 400 in the second. However, that has been just one of the two draws in 15 Tests the venue has hosted, with New Zealand winning nine. India vs New Zealand | Seasoned K L Rahul and young Yashasvi Jaiswal are rubbing off on each other’s success India, as skipper Shubman Gill indicated in the post-match press conference on Monday, are likely to field the same XI for the second game as well. The only possible change could be Gurnoor Brar coming in place of Anshul Kamboj. Brar impressed in the preceding one-day series. However, given how invaluable experience is, especially in such a crunch game, India would be better off playing Mohammed Siraj. The Hyderabadi bowled his heart out during the series in Australia and England, and he’s the sort of seamer who can make things happen when the chips are down. Even when he isn’t bowling, you can see him giving a pep talk to others, often lifting drooping shoulders. Hopefully, the management, which appears to have lost faith in his ability following an ordinary series in Sri Lanka, will reconsider its stance. New Zealand, who fly to Australia for four Tests starting December 9 in Perth, would be hoping to extend their impressive record here. Not only would it strengthen their position in the WTC table, but it would also give them a chance to avenge their series losses in the T20Is and ODIs prior to the Tests. They were outplayed in the T20Is, while India showed good nerve to nick the ODIs. Victory in the Test will give them something to smile about. India, on the other hand, will be gunning for a perfect treble. If Gill and Co win the Test series, they’ll become just the third Indian side to win a Test series in New Zealand. They’ll be gunning for exactly that. New Zealand: Tom Latham (C), Tom Blundell (WK), Devon Conway, Jacob Duffy, Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips, Rachin Ravindra, Nathan Smith, Will Young, Dean Foxcroft, Matt Fisher.

Jensen Huang is back, and so is the open-weight AI debate in Washington
articles.summary: Nvidia's leadership crisis has thrust a tech industry squabble over open-weight AI models into the spotlight, where CEO Jensen Huang has become one of Washington's loudest voices for US development of a technology now dominated by Chinese companies. Nvidia’s board announced on Monday that it would reinstate Huang as CEO, following his resignation over reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman who news reports said was suspected of spying for the Chinese government. Before the scandal erupted, Huang had pushed the US Congress and the Trump administration to support American companies developing open-weight AI models, which would align with his company’s commercial interests, although a debate has raged over the models' implications for US national security. President Donald Trump's administration supports open-weight AI systems because they give startups dependable and cheaper options outside proprietary AI tools from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. “The Trump Administration’s clear and long-standing policy has been strong support for” open-weight AI models, a White House official said in a statement to Reuters on Tuesday. Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang in part because they viewed him as the protector of US-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday. The White House did not comment on the connection between the support for Huang and open-weight models. Open-weight AI models, unlike closed models, make core components publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Such models broaden demand for Nvidia’s chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of leading AI model developers, providing a business opportunity for Huang’s company. Executives from closed-model developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI have expressed skepticism of open-weight models, according to their public statements, creating a schism in the AI sector. Anthropic and OpenAI earn revenue by selling access to proprietary systems whose underlying technology they control. "Any kind of political headwinds against Huang and Nvidia could be a harbinger for a crackdown on open weights, which is not good for little tech and companies that are trying to have a fighting chance of disrupting some of the incumbents,” said Luther Lowe of Y Combinator, a Silicon Valley incubator and startup fund. Taiwan is psyched that Jensen Huang is back in the driver's seat at Nvidia In a letter earlier this year, Huang urged the US government to avoid "premature restrictions" on open-weight tools. A coalition of companies co-signed the letter, including venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, Microsoft and Palantir. Anthropic declined to sign on. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said he disagreed with parts of Huang’s statement, arguing that increasingly capable open-weight models could create security risks, including helping users to exploit publicly available information to develop biological weapons. In a statement, he said that "sufficiently capable" AI tools could use publicly available materials to spread infectious diseases. US competitiveness with China is also a key aspect of the policy debate in Washington. Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Alibaba's offerings have won American business users because they are often cheaper than proprietary systems from OpenAI and Anthropic while performing comparably on many tasks. The Trump administration has taken a few steps to support the US open-weight ecosystem, including public statements from White House tech adviser Michael Kratsios. The Trump administration over the summer told leading AI model developers that it would not put open-weight AI models through voluntary government safety tests, Reuters reported, a win for proponents such as Nvidia who do not want such models to face additional regulatory hurdles. The administration is separately considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese-made AI models, including open-weight tools, Reuters reported last week. Two Republican chairs of House committees involved in AI policy urged the Trump administration last week to go further, by barring US government agencies and contractors from using Chinese open-weight AI models. They want the government to give US companies developing open-weight models more access to computing resources, arguing that expanding the open-weight ecosystem in the US is a national security imperative in the AI race against China. "The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so," House Homeland Security Committee chair Andrew Garbarino and China Committee chair John Moolenaar said in a joint statement.

Chine's Huawei convicted in US trial over Iran business, trade secrets theft
articles.summary: Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it had deceived banks about its business in Iran and stolen trade secrets from US companies. A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced. The jury found the technology company not guilty of racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging it had acted as a criminal enterprise. In a statement, Huawei said the charges on which it was convicted lack legal merit and said it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests." US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks. The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology. Experts have said the case has nonetheless not undermined Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence. The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15. Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice. Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial. "After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during her closing argument. Founder's daughter had been detained The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada. Meng had been secretly indicted on charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions. She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped. Prosecutors alleged trade secrets theft The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran. HSBC upgrades Indian equities to 'overweight', cuts China to ‘neutral’ Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades. During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX. Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device. Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify. Defence says banks knew of Iran business The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for Huawei's business. Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. He said Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development." The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina's Dec 16 return gambit could redraw Bangladesh's political battlelines, test India ties
articles.summary: New Delhi: Sheikh Hasina's Awami League on Tuesday announced that Bangladesh's deposed prime minister would return to her country from India on December 16, a date carefully chosen for its historical and political significance, as well as to galvanise her party's cadres at a time when Tarique Rahman's government in Dhaka is already grappling with unrest in several districts. December 16 is a day inextricably linked to the shared history of Bangladesh and India. It was on this day in 1971 that East Pakistan broke free from Pakistan and emerged as the new nation of Bangladesh. It is celebrated as Victory Day on both sides of the border, commemorating the surrender of the Pakistan Army's Eastern Command to the joint command of the Indian and Bangladeshi forces, ending the nine-month-long Muktijuddha . Hasina has chosen the day to reclaim the legacy of the 'Liberation War' of Bangladesh, rooted in its secular, linguistic and cultural identity, which distinguished its founding ideals from the religious identity underpinning Pakistan. She is not only invoking the history of 1971 and subtly underlining India's decisive role in the birth of Bangladesh, but also seeking to reclaim a political legacy closely identified with her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and the Awami League. It is also an attempt to restore her and her party's historical legitimacy and counter allegations of authoritarianism against her by projecting both as inheritors of the liberation struggle and the secular ideals of Bangladesh. New Delhi has been sticking to its position that Dhaka's request for her extradition from India is a "legal matter". It has not yet reacted to Hasina's plan to return to Bangladesh on December 16. Dhaka, however, has adopted a far more combative position. Humaiun Kobir, the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs in the Bangladesh Nationalist Party's government, said that the former prime minister could be brought back only "in handcuffs or under strict surveillance". His colleague, Shama Obaed Islam, said that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government would treat the Awami League chief under the same laws applicable to any other convicted fugitive staying abroad, adding that she would be arrested upon entering Bangladesh. Whether Hasina will return or not is an issue Dhaka would discuss with New Delhi, not with the deposed prime minister, Rahman's Information and Broadcasting Adviser, Zahed Ur Rahman, said. With many of its leaders arrested and its activities banned, the Awami League was pushed to the political margins after its government collapsed in the wake of the mass protests that swept Bangladesh in July and August 2024. It was also barred from participating in the February 2026 parliamentary elections, which the BNP won, defeating its former ally, Jamaat-e-Islami (JI). However, since Hasina, who had flown to the Indian Air Force base in Hindon near Delhi in an aircraft of the Bangladesh Air Force on August 5, 2024, announced earlier this year her plan to return to her country, the party has been reasserting its presence on the streets. On Tuesday, after her spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali declared December 16 as the date for her return, the party started projecting it as " Dwitiya Muktijuddhe Dwitiya Vijay " (second victory in the second Liberation War) and called upon its cadres across the country to prepare to welcome the " Ganamanusher Netri " (Leader of the Masses). In a move suggesting that she wants to turn her proposed return into more than a political declaration, Hasina has formally sought travel documents from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi. According to her spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, her lawyer sent communications to the mission on November 9 and 19 seeking the necessary documents. She has also asked the Dhaka government to arrange her return on the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh, arguing that since she was flown to India aboard a military aircraft of Bangladesh on August 5, 2024, the BNP government in Dhaka should facilitate her journey back in the same manner, on an aircraft of her country's national carrier. Hasina left Bangladesh a few hours before her Awami League government collapsed amid mass protests, initially triggered by student and youth demonstrations against the reservation system in government jobs and intensified by a police crackdown on protesters. A court in Dhaka had, on November 17, 2025, awarded Hasina the death sentence for the "crimes against humanity" committed during the police crackdown on protesters in July 2024. Bangladesh's then interim government had subsequently sought her extradition from India. New Delhi's ties with Dhaka had been on a positive trajectory during Hasina's tenure as prime minister. But bilateral relations became strained after the collapse of the Awami League government. Sheikh Hasina eyes Bangla Victory Day return; Dhaka dangles handcuffs India's concerns over attacks on the religious minority community, the growing influence of radical Islamist forces in Bangladesh and the ban on the Awami League, alongside its repeated calls for inclusive elections, strained relations. Dhaka's insistence on Hasina's extradition from India also emerged as an irritant in bilateral ties. New Delhi subsequently reached out to the BNP and sought to build a pragmatic relationship with Tarique Rahman's government in Dhaka. However, Hasina's virtual interaction with journalists in New Delhi, during which she announced plans to return from India and accused the post-August 2024 governments of undermining the secular foundations of Bangladesh, triggered a sharp diplomatic backlash from Dhaka and renewed calls for her extradition. Rahman's reluctance to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi dealt a setback to efforts to restore normalcy in bilateral ties. Hasina's proposed return appears to be bringing the BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) and the National Citizens Party (NCP) closer, at least on the question of preventing the Awami League's political rehabilitation. Signs of this convergence have already emerged. Tarique Rahman met a four-member NCP delegation led by Nahid Islam on Monday, with discussions focusing on countering the Awami League's resurgence. The NCP demanded a complete ban on the Awami League. JI chief Shafiqur Rahman, meanwhile, cut short his overseas tour and returned to Dhaka on Tuesday for talks with the prime minister. Tarique and Shafiqur had also pledged in Parliament last week to work together against fascism. Hasina's proposed return could give this emerging convergence a sharper political purpose, bringing together forces that were instrumental in opposing her rule but have their own competing political ambitions. Rahman's government is also grappling with mounting economic discontent, particularly in the garment sector, which is central to Bangladesh's export economy. Workers have taken to the streets over wages, rising living costs, layoffs and demands for better working conditions, with demonstrations disrupting factory operations and triggering clashes and road blockades. The labour unrest has added to the government's law-and-order burden just as the Awami League is attempting to regain its presence on the streets through demonstrations against the ban on its activities and in support of Hasina's return. The two streams of discontent have different origins, but together they risk stretching the government's ability to manage competing pressures on the streets. For the ruling BNP, the challenge is to prevent the Awami League from exploiting the prevailing disquiet to rebuild its political base while addressing the genuine economic grievances fuelling workers' protests. The Bangladesh Army remains an important and potentially unpredictable power centre. Its response to any escalation of street protests will be closely watched, as will its position on the BNP government's approach towards the Awami League. Whether the army will remain a passive observer if Hasina and her party attempt a political resurgence in Bangladesh is an open question. The next three weeks could therefore prove consequential for Bangladesh's internal politics as well as its relations with India. Hasina may or may not return to Dhaka on December 16, but her announcement has already set in motion a political contest whose repercussions could extend well beyond Victory Day.

In July, the Trump administration imposed import duties of 10% or 12.5% on goods from those 60 trading partners. They are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia. It was unclear what tariff rates would be charged on imports, or what exemptions may be granted. The probe is partly directed at Chinese investment into countries in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid tariffs. Under a US-China trade truce due to expire on January 10, the Trump administration has capped second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20 per cent, in addition to duties of about 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5 per cent anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5 per cent to reach the 20 per cent cap.
